title: Budget alerts versus enforced usage limits

opening.headline: The budget alert indicates the difference between the device that notifies and the device that actually stops increasing costs.
body: We set a warning threshold at a monthly budget of $1,000, and after the threshold was exceeded, an email was sent. While someone received the email, no one stopped using the service, and costs continued to rise, ultimately exceeding the monthly budget. The alert only notifies; it does not stop usage.

This course distinguishes between alerts and actual limits and confirms the scope of capabilities available on each platform. It first examines Databricks' budget and billing usage tables, Snowflake's resource monitoring and budgeting, and user-specific quotas, then proceeds in sequence to review cases where alerts are present but no limits exist, leading to overuse.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain budget alerts and usage limitations features of Databricks and Snowflake
You can analyze costs that remain outside control by examining the scope of application by category.

screens.title: Budget alerts have come in, yet costs have continued to rise.
screens.lead: First, examine the scenario where costs continue to increase even after an alert has been received. Compare the alert timestamp with the end-of-month overrun point in the diagram.

visual.alt: With monthly budget line and cumulative cost curve, and an alert icon at the point where the threshold is exceeded, a graph showing significant overage at month-end.

paragraphs: We set the monthly budget to $1,000 and configured a notification threshold. Once the cost exceeded the threshold, an email was sent. Someone has read that email.

Yet no one stopped the service, and there was no procedure to do so. Costs continued to rise thereafter, ultimately exceeding the budget by the end of the month. The issue was not that the notifications failed in their role, but that the role expected of them was fundamentally incorrect from the outset.

Notifications inform users. Disabling functionality serves the purpose of restriction. This course distinguishes between notifications and restrictions, and examines which mechanisms on each platform provide only notifications and which actually enable disabling, as well as the scope of application for each mechanism.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When a budget alert occurs, who is instructed to do what? Without a process, the alert is not a cost-reducing mechanism but merely a record indicating that costs have increased.

screens.outro: First, let's recall whether we are distinguishing between notifications and restrictions when setting them up.

screens.title: Do you want to set alerts and restrictions separately?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Since you're not entering an answer, first recall your environment and then try it.

items.prompt: What is defined for whom to perform actions when a threshold is reached?
items.answer: If only alerts are configured, it must be specified what action the recipient of the alert should take. Without defining whether to reduce service, switch models, or report to a responsible party, the alert cannot translate into actionable steps.

items.prompt: How far does the automatic restriction apply?
items.answer: Limited capabilities are applied to specific targets depending on the platform. Some capabilities apply only to warehouses, while others apply only to requests passing through specific gateways. Costs outside of these scopes increase regardless of any limitations applied.

items.prompt: Is the feature that incurs the highest cost within the scope of control?
items.answer: This is the most important question: if a feature that consumes a significant portion of the cost is outside the scope, then control is essentially nonexistent. This course examines the scope of each approach individually.

screens.outro: Now, let's check the budget of Databricks and the scope of alerts and suppression.

screens.title: Databricks: Budget and billing usage system tables
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted below, a brief description appears. Review each term one by one to see how the budget divides alerts and blocking.

visual.alt: Budget definition, thresholds and email, blocking options within Unity Gateway scope, configuration diagram continuing with billing usage system tables.
labels: Scope: Workspace, Resource Type, Custom Tag
Maximum of 4 threshold values, email specified

data.text: Databricks budget tracks spending on an entire account or specific teams, projects, or workspaces at list prices in USD. The scope can be narrowed down by workspace, resource type, or custom tags, and up to four monthly thresholds can be set. Email addresses can be specified for each threshold to receive alerts when spending exceeds the limit; account administrator privileges are required to create a budget. General budget sends only notifications.. The option to actually block requests when thresholds are reached, Block usage, is only available in Unity Gateway scope budget and includes per-user thresholds within this scope. Unity Gateway scope budget handles pay-per-token, ai_query, Genie, and separate options for external model usage. Provisioned throughput requests are not traced.. Post-analysis uses the system.billing.usage system table, which contains billing usage data such as sku_name, usage_date, custom_tags, and usage_quantity, typically reflected within 12 hours. Budget alert emails include the budget name and tags, thus Do not include sensitive information in tags..

terms.tip: The basic action of the budget is to send an email to the specified email address when the threshold is exceeded. It does not halt expenditures.
This option blocks additional requests through Unity Gateway when a threshold is reached. It can only be enabled within the Unity Gateway scope budget.
This is a budget designated as a Unity Gateway resource. It tracks expenditures passing through the gateway endpoint and narrows down the target using tags attached to the endpoint.

terms.term: Provisioned throughput requests are not traced.
terms.tip: This falls outside the scope of the Unity Gateway budget. If a significant portion of the costs is attributed to this request, simply blocking this budget will not be sufficient.
This is a system table that aggregates a user's billed usage. It includes SKU, usage date, custom tags, and usage for post-analysis.

terms.term: Do not include sensitive information in tags.
terms.tip: Tag data is stored as plain text and can be replicated globally. Do not use names or values that could affect personal information or security.

screens.outro: Having verified Databricks' scope, I will now present a table comparing Snowflake's three methods.

screens.title: Snowflake: Resource Monitor, Budget, User-specific Queries
screens.lead: The following table compares four cost control mechanisms available in Snowflake. For each row, verify the target and action, and determine whether the mechanism is an alert or a block.

data.caption: Scope and Operation of Snowflake Cost Control Features
rows: Credit usage for virtual warehouse and the cloud services that support it
It operates when limits or thresholds are reached. Serverless function and AI service expenses are not tracked.
Monthly limit for accounts or custom object bundles
Alerts at threshold values, custom actions via stored procedure
Evaluates periodically, with a maximum of 8 hours from exceeding the threshold to action, and up to 2 hours under delay optimization mode.
Track AI credits for functions such as AI Functions and Cortex Agents at the team or cost center level
Alert: Custom actions using stored procedure
Tag users to group them into teams. They are evaluated periodically, such as on a budget basis.
Credit limit per user. One quarter tracks either the warehouse or the AI domain.
AI domain usage can be blocked; warehouse provides tracking and alerts
Blocking is applied within a few minutes and is automatically released when the period expires. Limits are applied separately for each user and are not aggregated.
data.notes: The Resource Monitor is dedicated to the warehouse, so serverless function credits and AI service credits must be viewed within the budget. Quota provides AI cost control that can block costs without requiring a separate stored procedure; however, the blocking evaluation occurs after expenditure and within a few days, allowing slight overages of the limit. If a user with a 100-credit quota has 10 users, they can collectively spend up to 1,000 credits. If a single shared limit is needed, use a budget.

screens.outro: Having examined the scope of both platforms, we will now review the cases where alerts were present but no restrictions existed, in the order of our inspection.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Notifications only, with no restrictions, leading to overage cases
screens.lead: We break down a case where AI costs increased despite instructors setting controls on two platforms, step by step. Select the next arrow to proceed in the order of checking the scope of each approach.

visual.alt: The cost area is divided into notification zones, block zones, and areas outside control on a scope map.
labels: Alert region: Databricks General Budget, Snowflake Budget

Outside of control: provisioned throughput request, AI costs outside of warehouse (resource monitoring based)

steps.title: Situation: Control has been put in place, yet AI costs have increased.
steps.body: In Databricks, we set budget alerts using team tags, and in Snowflake, we enabled resource monitoring on the warehouse. However, AI function call costs have been continuously increasing. With both controls in place, we now examine the scope to understand why costs have risen.

steps.title: Step 1: Databricks Check - Alert or Blocked?
steps.body: Only the Unity Gateway scope budget allows enabling Block usage in a budget. General budgets created with team tags only send email notifications. Therefore, if a person does not take action when a notification is received, costs will not be stopped.

steps.title: Stage 2 Scope Review: What is being tracked?
steps.body: The Unity Gateway budget covers pay-per-token, ai_query, Genie, and the use of external models with separate options enabled. If a significant portion of the cost relates to provisioned throughput, this budget does not track such requests. Costs that cannot be blocked, even when blocking is enabled, are still incurred.

steps.title: Step 3: Snowflake Audit - Scope of Resource Monitor
steps.body: Resource Monitor only watches the warehouse. The cost of AI functions falls outside the serverless environment, so it does not enter there. The monitor's lack of response is not a failure but rather because it was outside the scope.

steps.title: Step 4 Enhancement: Team Tracking and Individual Blocking
steps.body: AI costs are tracked on a team basis within a shared resource budget, and individual overages are blocked using user-specific quotas. Since quotas are applied separately per user, a combined ceiling is necessary when budgeting is shared across users. Additionally, quota enforcement is applied after evaluation within a time window, not at request time, which means limits can be slightly exceeded.

steps.title: Step 5: Post-Analysis - Verify Where the Increase Occurred
steps.body: You can check the billing usage system table to determine which tag has exceeded its limit. For example, aggregate by tag as in `SELECT usage_date, custom_tags['team'] AS team, SUM(usage_quantity) AS qty FROM system.billing.usage GROUP BY usage_date, custom_tags['team']`. Records are typically reflected within 12 hours, so usage from a few hours prior might not be visible.

steps.title: Conclusion: Notifications are delivered, limits are paused.
steps.body: Notifications inform people, while constraints cause the system to halt. It's important to combine both appropriately according to the objective and to assess what costs fall outside the scope of each mechanism. What matters more than the fact that controls are in place is the portion of cost that those controls actually cover.

screens.outro: We have completed the example; now I will summarize the key points and conclude.

screens.title: Core Summary: Notifications inform, limits stop.
screens.lead: We summarize the course content through a comparison of the two platforms. Begin by reading the material while recalling the end-of-month overrun from the first scene.

paragraphs: Alerts and restrictions serve different purposes. Alerts inform a person, while restrictions cause a system to halt usage. If there are only alerts, the recipient must take action for the cost to stop, so it must be predefined who will do what following the alert.

Databricks budgeting is primarily based on alerts, and actual blocking of requests occurs at the Unity Gateway level. This scope covers pay-per-token, ai_query, Genie, and external model usage enabled via separate options, but does not track provisioned throughput. Snowflake resource monitoring is warehouse-specific, and AI costs are tracked by team through shared resource budgets and enforced per-user quotas.

All methods have a scope, so costs outside that scope are not controlled. When designing controls, first verify that the feature with the highest cost is within the scope, and ensure that chargeable usage is aggregated by tag for post-analysis purposes.

callout.label: Check sequence
callout.text: First, we verify whether this feature is an alert or a block, then determine its scope of application, and finally confirm whether the highest cost falls within that scope.

glossary.def: A control mechanism that sends alerts by comparing expenditures against a threshold. Both Databricks and Snowflake start with alerts.
This is an option that blocks additional requests when a threshold is reached within the Unity Gateway budget range.
A system table containing Databricks billing usage, typically reflected within 12 hours.
An object that monitors and alerts or pauses credit usage in Snowflake's virtual warehouse.
Snowflake's AI cost control that allows setting credit limits and blocking usage per user.

misconceptions.myth: Once a budget is created, expenditures are automatically halted.
misconceptions.fact: The foundation of budgeting is notification. Blocking is an option that must be enabled within the supported scope; costs outside of that scope will not be halted.

misconceptions.myth: Snowflake's Resource Monitor can help control AI costs.
misconceptions.fact: Resource Monitor is dedicated to the warehouse. Serverless function and AI service expenditures are managed based on budget or user-specific quotas.

misconceptions.myth: The quarter stops precisely at the limit.
misconceptions.fact: Quota evaluation occurs after expenditure within a short period, so usage may slightly exceed the limit. Quotas are applied individually to each user and are not aggregated.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Notifications inform people, while restrictions cause the system to halt.
The Databricks budget blocking option is available within the Unity Gateway scope.
Snowflake Resource Monitor is dedicated to warehousing, and AI costs are managed according to budget and per-user quotas.
Control scope varies by situation, so it is necessary to review costs that fall outside of control.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What cost control measures am I using—alerts or restrictions—and what costs fall outside of this scope?
